item.research_question: Which equimolar quinary combinations of 40 metallic elements form thermodynamically stable single-phase solid solutions, and what are the driving factors (mixing enthalpy, melting point, intermetallic competition) governing their formation?
item.material_system: Equimolar quinary alloys from 40 elements (e.g., AlCoMnNiV, CoFeMnNiZn, Cantor alloy CoCrFeMnNi)
item.processing_route: High-throughput density-functional theory (DFT) calculations using a binary regular solid-solution model; experimental synthesis via arc-melting (AlCoMnNiV) and mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering (CoFeMnNiZn)
item.test_conditions: Thermodynamic stability assessed at temperatures ranging from 800 to 1600 K, with optimal screening at T = 0.9Tm; experimental validation via SEM, XRD, and EDS after heat treatment at 1373 K (AlCoMnNiV) and 1073–1273 K (CoFeMnNiZn)
key_findings: Identified 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys out of 658,008 candidates (4.6% of combinations).
74% of the predicted stable HEAs form in body-centered cubic (BCC) structures.
The model achieved a predictive accuracy of 74% at T = 1350 K, outperforming empirical rules and free-energy models.
High melting point (Tm) is the primary driving factor for HEA formation, with nearly 80% of predicted HEAs containing at least one refractory element.
Al and Zn are outliers that form HEAs easily despite low melting points (933 K and 692 K, respectively) due to favorable mixing with high-melting elements.
The mixing enthalpy of solid solutions correlates linearly with the formation enthalpy of competing intermetallics (IMs).
Successfully synthesized and confirmed the existence of BCC AlCoMnNiV (lattice parameter 2.9 Å) and FCC CoFeMnNiZn (lattice parameter 3.635 Å).
The model predicts that substituting Cr with Zn in the Cantor alloy yields the most stable FCC single-phase HEA among Zn-containing variants.
item.mechanism: Phase stability is determined by the competition between the Gibbs free energy of the solid solution (driven by configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy) and the free energy of competing intermetallic phases. High melting points allow for high synthesis temperatures where entropic stabilization dominates, while mild mixing enthalpy often correlates with weak intermetallic competition, facilitating solid solution formation.
item.limitations: The model does not account for vibrational entropy, magnetic ordering, or short-range ordering, which would increase computational cost; it also struggles to discriminate between HCP and FCC structures due to their small energy difference.
item.future_work: Future screenings can incorporate vibrational effects, magnetic ordering, and short-range ordering in a tiered approach; the model can be applied to non-equimolar compositions and tailored for specific properties beyond phase stability.
quotes: We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures.

The stability of the alloys can be clearly discriminated from the PCA scores. It is apparent that the stability is mainly correlated with the melting point and, to a lesser extent, with the competing IMs and the mixing enthalpy of solid solutions.

We demonstrate the power of our method by predicting the existence of two new high-entropy alloys, i.e. the body-centered cubic AlCoMnNiV and the face-centered cubic CoFeMnNiZn, which are successfully synthesized.
